entries.title: Man hospitalized after being shot during argument in Fuller Park
entries.summary: <p>A man was fatally shot Thursday night in Fuller Park, according to Chicago police.</p><p>The man, 39, and another man were in a verbal altercation inside a residence in the 5300 block of South Shields Avenue at 9:35 p.m. when they started physically fighting and the other man fired shots, police said. The 39-year-old was shot in his face and was taken to University of Chicago Medical Center in critical condition.</p><p>No one is in custody.</p>
entries.author: Sun-Times Wire

entries.title: Two men fatally shot in Dunning
entries.summary: <p>Two men were killed Thursday afternoon in a shooting in Dunning, according to Chicago police.</p><p>The men were found behind a residence in the 7800 block of West Cahill Terrace at 3:30 p.m., police said. One of the men, who was 20-years-old was shot multiple times and taken to Lutheran General Hospital where he was pronounced dead.</p><p>The other man, whose age wasn’t known, was taken to the same hospital in critical condition and later died.</p><p>No one is in custody.<br></p>
entries.author: Sun-Times Wire

entries.title: Man shot as he exits vehicle in Near West Side neighborhood
entries.summary: <p>A man was shot Thursday afternoon in the Near West Side neighborhood, according to Chicago police.</p><p>The man, 41, was getting out of a vehicle in the 500 block of South Claremont Avenue at 2:40 p.m when a white sedan approached and someone inside fired several shots, police said. He was taken to Stroger Hospital in critical condition.</p><p>No one is in custody.</p>
entries.author: Sun-Times Wire

entries.title: CPS says it won’t cut instructional time or Safe Passage program in upcoming budget
entries.summary: <p>Chicago Public Schools officials say there are some services that won’t be touched as the district works to plug a projected $732 million deficit for the upcoming school year.</p><p>That includes crossing guards and the Safe Passage program, which provides workers around schools to keep students safe during arrival and dismissal. Partnerships with organizations that provide mentoring to students, such as Youth Guidance and City Year, will also be preserved.</p><p>And CPS CEO and Supt. Macquline King said the district would not reduce instructional time for students to plug the budget gap, though Chicago Teachers Union officials have said they were told in meetings with the district that a shortened school year was under consideration.</p><p>Still, district officials admit it will be a challenge to keep cuts away from the classroom. Emila Zoko, the acting chief budget officer, said Thursday that the district had asked “department leaders to determine what reductions can be made with the least impact on students.”</p><p>But “it’s getting harder and harder to make reductions” that don’t “impact direct student programming and student supports,” she said.</p><p>In May, the district announced plans to <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/education/2026/05/12/cps-plans-cut-teacher-positions-raise-class-sizes-shrink-723-million-deficit" target="_blank" ><u>reduce the number of regular teachers</u></a> in the 2026-27 school year by raising the student-to-teacher ratio it uses to provide funding to schools. Many schools are losing their assistant principals and other positions.</p><p>The district is still working on its budget plan for next school year, but it’s planning at least $105 million in cuts to non-classroom costs, such as reducing the number of custodians and central office staffers.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>A crossing guard helps students get to Melody Elementary safely in August 2023. CPS officials have said they won’t cut crossing guards or the Safe Passage program in the upcoming school year.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Mark Black/For the Sun-Times file</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>The district also plans to add special education teachers, classroom assistants and physical therapists for students with disabilities, though those staff typically provide services that are required under federal law to meet students’ needs.</p><p>The CTU claims the district is considering reducing the number of school days next year to save money. Jackson Potter, vice president of the union, said that’s on top of proposed cuts to librarians, tech coordinators and athletic directors.</p><p>“In discussions with the district and the city, we are hearing that up to two weeks of the school year could be canceled in order to meet the budget gap that will still exist after these cuts have been imposed,” Potter said Thursday.</p><p>But the district denied that option was on the table. A CPS spokesperson wrote in a statement that “at no point has the District considered shortening the school year to alleviate these financial challenges.”</p><p>And King assured parents at Thursday’s school board meeting that CPS “will not limit instructional time for students next year” based on budget constraints.</p><p>CPS said it plans to release next year’s proposed budget plan by July 15 and is holding a series of community roundtable discussions before then.</p><p>Ahead of Thursday’s meeting, Potter and other members of the CTU called on state lawmakers to hold a special legislative session to increase funding for CPS. According to the state’s school funding formula, CPS gets 73% of what it needs to provide an “adequate education.” The district would be in a surplus if the state met its funding obligations, CTU members said.</p><p>Higher costs, including maintenance of the district’s aging facilities, labor agreements and CPS debt payments are contributing to the deficit. Additionally, property tax payments <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/money/2026/06/09/cook-county-property-tax-bills-delay-preckwinkle" target="_blank" ><u>were delayed again this year</u></a>, costing CPS much-needed funds, officials said.</p><p>Property taxes are the district’s single-largest revenue source. Without timely payments, CPS is forced to take out billions in short-term loans to pay staff and keep the lights on, <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/education/2025/12/19/property-tax-payment-delay-costs-chicago-public-schools-almost-a-quarter-million-dollars-a-day" target="_blank" ><u>resulting in millions of dollars in interest payments</u></a>. That’s money that doesn’t get spent on classrooms.</p><p>Several community members spoke out against planned cuts at their schools.</p><p>Andrew Kaplan, a parent and local school council member at Whitney Young High School, said the school is set to lose seven teaching and student support positions compared to last year due to the new student-to-teacher ratio.</p><p>Langston Ellis, a rising senior at the school, said that will lower the quality of the education.</p><p>“I have no doubt that our teachers and administrators will do all they can to support the students,” Ellis said, “but the harsh reality is that programs are being cut, livelihoods are being affected.”</p>

entries.title: Cubs' Pedro Ramirez plays through sadness, worry as countrymen deal with aftermath of Venezuela earthquakes
entries.summary: <p>NEW YORK — After an earthquake struck Venezuela on Wednesday, <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs" >Cubs</a> infielder <b>Pedro Ramirez</b> was relieved to get confirmation from his mother that his family was OK.</p><p>When a second earthquake struck and things got worse in his home country, the 22-year-old once again reached for his phone to check in on his loved ones.</p><p>This time, he didn’t get the same quick reassurance.</p><p>“During the [second game of Wednesday’s doubleheader, injured Venezuelan reliever <b>Daniel] Palencia</b> had told me that the situation got much worse,” Ramirez said through an interpreter Thursday. “After the game, I texted my mom, and she didn’t immediately respond to me. So there was some worry there.</p><p>“She eventually did respond to me, and I was able to get in touch with her. … Thank god my family’s safe. But still, I’m really sad for everything that we’re going through.</p><p>“There’s a lot of deaths, a lot of children [affected] and a lot of people that were left without a home. We’re fine, but we’re still sad with everything that has occurred.”</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/nation-world/2026/06/24/back-to-back-powerful-earthquakes-slam-venezuela-collapsing-buildings-in-the-capital-of-caracas" >Powerful earthquakes hit Venezuela, collapsing buildings in Caracas and shaking up Chicagoan relatives</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p>Such was the experience for the proud Venezuelan a continent away from <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/nation-world/2026/06/24/back-to-back-powerful-earthquakes-slam-venezuela-collapsing-buildings-in-the-capital-of-caracas" >the devastating natural disaster</a> that’s claimed more than 150 lives and has negatively impacted so many more.</p><p>In addition to Ramirez and Palencia, the Cubs’ Venezuelan contingent includes catcher <b>Moises Ballesteros</b>, currently playing in the minor leagues, as well as infield coach <b>Jonathan Mota</b> and bullpen catcher <b>Erick Castillo</b>.</p><p>“We’re all Venezuelan,” Ramirez said, “and we’re all sharing that pain together.”</p><p>Ramirez and Palencia wore caps with “VZ” on the side during Thursday night’s game, an important showing of solidarity with their impacted countrymen.</p><p>“It’s a way to show that we’re there with them and that everything that they’re feeling, we’re feeling as well,” Ramirez said. “All the Venezuelans outside of the country, we’re all feeling that.”</p><p>This moment in his country’s history is a tough one to be away from as his family and so many others deal with the aftermath.</p><p>But being away from home is, sadly, nothing new for Ramirez as he’s chased his baseball dream.</p><p>“I left home at 12 years old to play. I’ve learned to live like that, to be away from them,” Ramirez said. “It’s difficult because you’re far away from them, and whenever they don’t respond to you, you always get worried because you don’t know what happens to your family once you’re far away.”</p><p>Thankfully, Ramirez now knows his family is OK. But his heart is with the Venezuelans who are still looking for that same reassurance and those who aren’t able to find it.</p><h3><b>Brown down</b></h3><h3></h3><p>Cubs righty pitcher <b>Ben Brown</b> is going through some unfortunate deja vu dealing with a stress reaction in his neck that’s being described as similar to the injury that wiped out the second half of his 2024 season.</p><p>The team sent Brown back to Chicago to get checked out and will get a second opinion before setting what team president <b>Jed Hoyer</b> called “a plan of attack.”</p><p>“It’s going to be a somewhat lengthy process of rest,” Hoyer said before Thursday’s game. “That injury, you can’t do much. You have to rest it. And we have to figure out how long that rest period is.”</p><h3><b>Boyd back</b></h3><h3></h3><p>Cubs lefty <b>Matthew Boyd</b> threw 76 pitches in 4⅔ innings in his long-awaited return from the injured list Thursday.</p><p>The 2025 All Star dealt with a lot of traffic on the bases, allowing four hits and walking four batters, but he kept the Mets off the scoreboard.</p><bsp-listcarousel
